Try gentle yoga, deep breathing exercises, or a warm bath before bed to help ease tension. Even a short walk outdoors can lift your mood and reduce discomfort.

Diet matters too. Focus on whole foods rich in calcium, magnesium, and vitamin B6, which may help ease symptoms naturally. Bananas, leafy greens, nuts, and seeds are all excellent choices. Cutting back on salty foods can reduce bloating, and staying well-hydrated helps flush out excess sodium.

If your symptoms feel overwhelming or interfere with daily life, don't hesitate to talk to a healthcare provider. Severe PMS could point to premenstrual dysphoric disorder, a condition that may require targeted treatment. You don't have to simply endure it — relief is available, and asking for support is a sign of strength, not weakness.

pair.human_continuation: Deep breathing exercises,  meditation, and  yoga are all good ways to relax.  Other ideas for stress-busting activities include writing in a journal, taking walks in nature, or calling up a friend for a chat. It’s not just in your head: when you’re stressed out, your cortisol levels rise, which can throw your hormonal balance out of whack and make your PMS  symptoms worse. When you’re not feeling your best, a little treat can make a big difference in your mood. Indulge in your favorite chocolates, a new book you’ve been eyeing, or a relaxing afternoon listening to your favorite music. Getting a massage, facial, or pedicure can take your mind off your PMS symptoms and lift your mood. Don’t feel like going out to a spa?

Caffeine can also contribute to headaches and insomnia. And while you might feel tempted to reach for a glass of wine if you have PMS, it’s better to resist the urge: alcohol can exacerbate mood swings and make cramps worse.
PMS symptoms like anxiety and irritability flare up more when you’re stressed. Give yourself a break and find ways to stay calm and cool-headed during this time of the month.
